title: NormedAddTorsor: The Abstract Setting for Euclidean Geometry
content:
The variables declaration establishes the proof's setting: a `NormedAddTorsor V P` — the abstract framework for Euclidean geometry in Lean 4/Mathlib. A torsor separates points ($P$, no privileged origin) from vectors ($V$, a vector space). The key operations are `vsub : P → P → V` (point subtraction, $A -_v B \in V$) and `vadd : V → P → P` (translation, $v +_v A \in P$). This is the mathematically clean way to do affine/Euclidean geometry: points don't have an origin, but differences of points are vectors.

By using `NormedAddTorsor` with `[InnerProductSpace ℝ V]`, the proof works in any Euclidean space of any dimension — not just $\mathbb{R}^2$. The isosceles triangle theorem (Euclid I.5) is thus proved once, for all Euclidean spaces simultaneously. The inner product structure `[InnerProductSpace ℝ V]` is what gives meaning to `InnerProductGeometry.angle` and provides the algebraic machinery for the proof.
mathContext: The `NormedAddTorsor V P` abstraction: $P$ is a torsor over vector space $V$; `vsub` and `vadd` satisfy $(v +_v p) -_v p = v$ and $p -_v q +_v q = p$. The `InnerProductSpace ℝ V` provides the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ needed to define angles: $\angle(u, v) = \arccos(\langle u,v \rangle / (\|u\| \cdot \|v\|))$.

title: vsub_eq_apex_diff: The Apex Vector Decomposition
content:
The lemma `vsub_eq_apex_diff` proves $C -_v B = (A -_v B) - (A -_v C)$ — the base vector equals the difference of the two apex vectors. Setting $p = A -_v B$ and $q = A -_v C$ (the 'apex vectors' pointing from the base vertices back to the apex), this says the base vector $C -_v B = p - q$. This is the algebraic key to Pappus's proof: the angle $\angle ABC$ (between $A -_v B$ and $C -_v B$) equals $\text{angle}(p, p-q)$, and $\angle ACB$ equals $\text{angle}(q, q-p)$, which are equal when $\|p\| = \|q\|$.

The proof of this lemma uses two torsor identities: `vsub_add_vsub_cancel C A B : (C -_v A) + (A -_v B) = C -_v B` and `neg_vsub_eq_vsub_rev A C : -(A -_v C) = C -_v A`. The `abel` tactic handles the abelian group arithmetic to assemble these.
mathContext: The lemma proves $C -_v B = (A -_v B) - (A -_v C)$. Proof: $(A -_v B) - (A -_v C) = (A -_v B) + -(A-_v C) = (A -_v B) + (C -_v A) = C -_v B$ by `vsub_add_vsub_cancel`. Setting $p = A-_v B$, $q = A-_v C$: $\angle ABC = \angle(p, p-q)$, $\angle ACB = \angle(q, q-p)$.
relatedConcepts: abel tactic for abelian group goals
prerequisites: abel tactic for linear arithmetic in abelian groups

title: pappus_isosceles: Four Lines Capturing 2000 Years of Insight
content:
The main theorem `pappus_isosceles` proves $\angle ABC = \angle ACB$ from $d(A,B) = d(A,C)$ in 4 lines. This is Pappus's self-congruence proof of Euclid I.5 (Pons Asinorum). The proof works by:
(1) `show` unfolds `EuclideanGeometry.angle` to `InnerProductGeometry.angle (A -_v B) (C -_v B) = ...` — necessary because Lean's unifier needs the two angle definitions explicitly equated.
(2) `rw [vsub_eq_apex_diff, vsub_neg_eq_apex_diff]` rewrites both base vectors as $p-q$ and $q-p$ where $p = A-_v B$, $q = A-_v C$.
(3) `apply InnerProductGeometry.angle_sub_eq_angle_sub_rev_of_norm_eq` — the Mathlib lemma that says $\text{angle}(p, p-q) = \text{angle}(q, q-p)$ when $\|p\| = \|q\|$. This is the algebraic crystallization of Pappus's SAS argument.
(4) `simpa only [← dist_eq_norm_vsub]` converts the distance hypothesis to the norm hypothesis.
mathContext: The Mathlib lemma used: `InnerProductGeometry.angle_sub_eq_angle_sub_rev_of_norm_eq : ‖x‖ = ‖y‖ → angle x (x-y) = angle y (y-x)`. Applied with $x = p = A-_v B$ and $y = q = A-_v C$: since $d(A,B) = d(A,C) \Leftrightarrow \|p\| = \|q\|$ (via `dist_eq_norm_vsub`), we get $\angle(p, p-q) = \angle(q, q-p)$, i.e., $\angle ABC = \angle ACB$.

title: euclid_outer_segs_eq: Step 1 of Euclid's Four-Step Proof
content:
The theorem `euclid_outer_segs_eq` formalizes the first step of Euclid's original proof of Pons Asinorum. Euclid's construction places points $F$ and $G$ beyond $B$ and $C$ on extensions of $AB$ and $AC$ with $AF = AG$. This lemma proves $BF = CG$ from $AF = AG$ and $AB = AC$.

In the algebraic formulation: if $F = A + s(B-A)$ and $G = A + t(C-A)$, then $AF = s \cdot AB$ and $AG = t \cdot AC$. From $AF = AG$ and $AB = AC$ we get $s = t$, so $BF = (s-1) \cdot AB = (t-1) \cdot AC = CG$. The `calc` block assembles this as a chain of equalities, with `ring` handling polynomial identities and `rw [hAB_eq_AC]` substituting the equal-side hypothesis.

Euclid's proof would then continue: prove $\triangle AFC \cong \triangle AGB$ (SAS), then $\triangle BFC \cong \triangle CGB$ (using $BF=CG$), then subtract angles. This file formalizes only Step 1 and the Pappus proof; the full Euclid proof is an open formalization task.
mathContext: Setup: $F = A + s \cdot (B-A)$, $G = A + t \cdot (C-A)$. Hypotheses: $|AF| = s|AB| = t|AC| = |AG|$ (from $AF=AG$) and $|AB| = |AC|$. Then $s = t$. Result: $|BF| = |s-1| \cdot |AB| = |t-1| \cdot |AC| = |CG|$.
prerequisites: Euclid's auxiliary construction for Pons Asinorum

title: euclid_i5: The Alias Connecting Both Names to One Proof
content:
`theorem euclid_i5 ... := pappus_isosceles h` is a one-line alias making the theorem discoverable under both names. The theorem statement is identical: `dist A B = dist A C → ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B`. The `#check @pappus_isosceles` and `#check @euclid_i5` commands serve as type documentation.

Naming the same result twice reflects the historical duality: the theorem statement is Euclid's (Elements I.5, ~300 BCE) but Pappus's proof (~340 AD) is simpler. In modern mathematics, the theorem is known as the *Pons Asinorum* ('Bridge of Asses') — the medieval name given because it was the first theorem in Euclid that separated students who could reason geometrically from those who could not. The 'bridge' had to be crossed to proceed further in Euclidean geometry.
mathContext: `euclid_i5 = pappus_isosceles`: identical statement `dist A B = dist A C → ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B`. Both names are in the `IsoscelesTriangleOQ01` namespace and are registered in Lean's type-checking environment via `#check`.
